pages.lede: This is the index for Wheaton. Underneath it sit six trades and four services, each written from what that particular job actually demands, plus the number of the person who would build it.

sections.h2: The county's business runs through here, and it brings a crowd that lives elsewhere.
paras: Wheaton holds 53,970 people and the county's institutions stacked on top of them. County offices stand at 421 N. County Farm Rd. The 18th Circuit courthouse is a short way along the same road at 505. On any given weekday there are people in town because a filing, a summons or a job put them here.

Add the College Avenue platform and the downtown station at 402 Front St, both feeding the Union Pacific West line, then a downtown calendar carrying more than 50 events a year, and the arithmetic turns uncomfortable for an owner. A good share of the people near your door today have never heard your business named out loud.

That is the entire argument for this set of pages. Goodwill carries a name across a dinner table. It does nothing at all inside the phone of somebody standing on Front Street for the first time this year.

sections.h2: Six trades, and each page was handed a different hard part.
paras: A shop with four chairs, a kitchen holding a party of thirty, a bay looking after somebody's vans — these are not one business in three uniforms, and writing them as though they were is how a website ends up saying nothing to anybody.

So every page below starts from the thing that decides that trade's year. Who the client book belongs to when a barber hands in notice. What a deposit does to a large party. Whether a service record survives a change of driver. Each one has a finished demo sitting behind it, with the booking switched on.

sections.h2: Four services, and the one to start with is the one that hurts.
paras: The online half of a business splits four ways. In a town where most owners are already trading perfectly well, it's rarely all four that need attention in the same month.
bullets: Website design — usually a rebuild here rather than a first attempt, because the site you own is four years old and quietly out of date.
Local SEO — you already come up for your own name, so the work is every search where nobody types it.
The CRM — three letters for the place your customer information is kept, and this one is angled at invoices, payments and what the month came to.
Booking and payments — availability a customer can trust, deposits that hold a slot, and a phone that stops being the only way in.

sections.h2: Both plans, both numbers, before you have to ask anybody.
paras: Foundation costs $250 a month and $250 once at the beginning. That buys the website itself on a domain that's yours, a Google Business Profile filled in the whole way, booking that lands on the calendar already in your pocket, email at your own address, the local search work, and two changes a month whenever you want them.

Growth costs $500 a month and $500 at the beginning, and adds the ledger underneath all of it — invoicing, card payments, automatic texts and emails, review requests, expenses, monthly reports and the accounting sync.

Settle twelve months in advance and 15 percent comes off, which puts the year at $2,550 or $5,100 with the build charged separately. Either plan will carry the two bolt-ons: round-the-clock call answering at $100 a month, automated Google review replies at $130. Anything unusual gets priced against the job itself and written down first.

The reason for the twelve months is arithmetic rather than a lock-in. A new site spends roughly its first three months earning nothing, and almost all of the building that matters happens inside that window.

sections.h2: Most businesses here aren't starting from nothing, and that changes the job.
paras: Owners in Wheaton tend to arrive with a website, a claimed profile, a respectable review count and years of goodwill behind them. What they're short of is rarely presence. It's the second half — the searches they never appear in, the estimate nobody chased, the invoice that left eleven days late.
So the four service pages here are written from that starting point rather than for a shop opening next month. If you're genuinely at zero, say so when you call and we'll aim somewhere else.

sections.h2: We're new, and the demos are the only evidence we have.
paras: There's no client roster on this site and no row of stars, because neither has been earned yet and you'd work that out on your own eventually.

Standing in their place are six finished businesses left switched on. Take a slot in the barbershop and the confirmation reaches your inbox in roughly ten seconds. That isn't a recording of a booking system; it is the booking system.
If all you want is a small site you'll update once a decade, cheap tools do that properly and we'll say so rather than talk you out of it.

pages.townPara: Wheaton College has stood on its 80-acre campus since 1860 and keeps about 2,800 students in the middle of everything else. Cantigny Park sits out at 1S151 Winfield Rd with the First Division Museum, the formal gardens and the golf. Cream of Wheaton fills four days at the start of June. None of that is trivia for an owner here — it's the reason an ordinary Tuesday contains people from three towns over, and why being known on your own street stopped being enough some time ago.

crmCallout.heading: Whichever page you open, the records underneath are the same.
crmCallout.para: It doesn't behave one way for a salon and another for a repair shop. What changes is which part of it you lean on: the barbershop cares who owns the client history, the landscape crew cares about staged payments, the restaurant cares about deposits on a room. The trade pages argue about that. The CRM page walks the whole thing end to end, from a booking taken at midnight to the page of numbers that lands on the first.

cta.heading: Ten doors, and something working behind each one.
cta.para: Open whichever page describes your week. If you'd sooner test something than read about it, the six demos are live and (331) 291-7400 gets you a person.

faqs.q: Do you work in Wheaton, or only in Glen Ellyn?
faqs.a: Both, and the towns between them. We work out of Glen Ellyn, one town east, and Wheaton has its own ten pages because the competition here has a different shape. The number is (331) 291-7400 and the email is jeffbilbrey@getprojectknox.com.

faqs.q: Which of these ten pages should I read first?
faqs.a: The one matching your trade, then the one matching whatever is currently broken. A shop losing a chair reads the barbershop page and then the CRM page. A business nobody can find reads the local SEO page and can stop there. Reading all ten was never the plan.

faqs.q: What do the two plans cost, and does Wheaton cost more?
faqs.a: No, and it doesn't cost less in Lombard either. Foundation is $250 monthly, after $250 to build it. Growth is $500 monthly, after $500 to build it. Twelve months paid in advance takes 15 percent off either, so $2,550 or $5,100 across the year, with the build billed on its own.

pages.lede: Ten pages for the Lilac Village: six trades and four services, written for owners who are currently working with a phone number, a sign, and not a great deal else online.

sections.h2: A village with a mall on one edge and a Main Street on the other.
paras: Yorktown Center opened in 1968 and runs to something like 1.5 million square feet. For a while it was the second-largest enclosed mall east of the Mississippi. A few minutes away, Main Street crosses St. Charles Road in a downtown you can walk end to end inside a coffee break.

Those two things pull at a business from opposite directions. Butterfield and the office corridor bring people who drove in from outside the village and will drive out again without registering what else is here. Downtown brings people who live four streets away and have known your sign for years.
Nearly every owner here is trying to be legible to both at once, and only one of the two can be reached by anything in a window.

sections.h2: Most of what we build here is the first version of everything.
paras: A number painted on a van. A Facebook page last touched in 2022. A Google listing somebody claimed years ago and never filled in, or one the search engine generated by itself that nobody has ever logged into. That's the common starting point in this village, and there's nothing embarrassing about it — the work has been arriving without any of it.

It does mean the first ninety days carry more weight than anything that happens afterward. The listing verified and sitting in your own account. Real prices on a page a stranger can read without ringing. A booking button live rather than promised. Every customer asked for a review from the first week rather than the first good quarter. All four service pages below are written from that standpoint.

sections.h2: What each of the six trade pages is actually about.
paras: A barbershop that opened in March and a landscape crew signing snow contracts in September have almost nothing in common, and neither of them needs a page explaining that websites matter.

So each one takes a single difficult part of that business and stays on it: the first forty haircuts, the lunch order placed at twenty to twelve, the fortnight after the first frost, the Saturday morning with six women and four chairs, the therapist deciding whether to send you her clients, the driveway agreed in autumn and cleared in January.

sections.h2: Four services, and you can buy them one at a time.
paras: Nobody needs all of this in month one, and suggesting otherwise would be a sales tactic rather than advice.
bullets: Website design — the first real site, on a domain registered to you, quick to open on a phone in a parking lot.
Local SEO — the Google Business Profile claimed, categorized, photographed and then genuinely maintained.
The CRM — the letters stand for customer relationship management, and in practice it's one list of who you serve, what they paid and when they're due back.
Booking and payments — an appointment page that works at eleven at night, and a card taken without a second machine on the counter.

sections.h2: The two numbers, and neither of them moves for your ZIP code.
paras: Foundation is $250 monthly with a single $250 build fee. That covers the website, the Google Business Profile, booking on the calendar you already keep, email at your own domain instead of a Gmail, the search work, and a couple of updates a month for the asking.

Growth is $500 monthly with a single $500 build fee, and switches on the customer ledger, invoicing, card payments, the automatic messages, review requests, expense tracking, the monthly report and the handoff to your accounting software.

A year paid at once removes 15 percent, so $2,550 or $5,100 for the twelve months, which reads as $212.50 and $425 a month with the build kept apart from it. Call answering runs $100 a month if the phone is beating you, review replies $130, and custom work gets a number in writing before anybody starts.
Twelve months on a fixed billing date, and no second invoice arriving from a different company halfway through the month.

If you enjoy this part — if you'd cheerfully spend a Sunday evening inside a site editor and would resent paying somebody else to do it — go and do that. The inexpensive tools are good, and you'd be buying back something you'd rather own yourself.

We're also new, which you should hear from us rather than deduce from the absence of logos. There are no client names on this site and no reviews of our own to point at. There are six complete businesses in the Vault instead, and four minutes inside one of them will tell you more than the rest of this page did.

pages.townPara: Lombard is 44,476 people inside a single ZIP code, 60148, with I-355 running down its western edge, I-88 along the south and North Avenue across the top. The Helen Plum Library and Glenbard East sit in the middle of that, and the Lombard Area Chamber of Commerce and Industry has spent years keeping the business side of it introduced to itself. What no map shows is the split in who walks through your door. One customer has passed your building a thousand times. The next came off an exit, bought one thing, and will never think about the village again.

crmCallout.heading: The list starts empty, which is the best possible reason to start it.
crmCallout.para: Behind the abbreviation is one place holding customers, appointments, invoices and expenses together. A business that has been run out of a phone and a spiral notebook has already lost years of that and can't get any of it back. From the week this is turned on, it's written down: who came in, what they paid, who hasn't been seen since spring. It's registered in your name, so it stays with you no matter what happens between us.

cta.heading: Use one of them properly before you call.
cta.para: Six businesses were built end to end and left running. Order lunch from the taqueria, book a cut, send yourself a landscape quote — whichever sits closest to your own work. Then ring (331) 291-7400.

faqs.q: We've never had a website. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: It's the ordinary case here, and it's easier than inheriting one somebody built badly in 2018. The slow part is usually the dull administration: getting the domain into your name, getting the listing verified, deciding what your services are really called. The building itself is quick.

faqs.q: Do you only work inside the village?
faqs.a: No. Lombard has its own ten pages because businesses here share a particular shape of problem, but we work across DuPage County generally, and out of Glen Ellyn next door.

faqs.q: Foundation or Growth if we're starting from scratch?
faqs.a: Foundation, usually, and we'd rather say that than sell upward. At $250 a month plus the $250 build it makes you findable and bookable, which is the piece that's missing. Growth at $500 a month plus $500 is the answer once the phone rings fine and the money side is what leaks. Moving up later turns parts on rather than starting again.

pages.formHeading: What have you got online right now?
pages.formSub: A listing, a Facebook page, nothing at all — tell us which, and we'll come back with where we would start and what it would cost.

pages.metaDescription: Website design, local SEO, online booking and a CRM for owner-run businesses in DuPage County, IL. Four county service pages, plus three town hubs.
pages.h1: Local websites, SEO and a CRM across DuPage County, Illinois
pages.lede: Four service pages written across the whole county, and three towns carrying sets of their own — Glen Ellyn, Wheaton and Lombard. Same builder, same two prices, and a county that behaves far less like one market than its outline suggests. One of the four is a CRM, and that abbreviation only ever described the place a business keeps track of who it has served.

sections.h2: Three towns, and the differences between them are not decoration.
paras: Glen Ellyn is a village of 28,846 that formally recognizes three separate business districts, which is a lot of variety for its size. Wheaton is the county seat at 53,970, holding the courts, a college and a downtown that stages more than 50 events a year. Lombard is 44,476 people with a tight Main Street on one side of it and a regional retail corridor doing most of the driving on the other.

Those differences decide what a website has to do. In one place the customer is already on the sidewalk and half decided. In another they're a stranger in town for a day. In the third they may never get out of the car at all.

So each town received its own ten pages, written separately, from that town's starting point. That took considerably longer than the alternative, and the alternative is the reason most local pages are worth nothing.

sections.h2: Nobody stays inside the town they live in.
paras: The county covers 336 square miles and moves on its roads. Four of them carry it east and west: I-88 as the Reagan Tollway, Roosevelt Road as IL 38, Butterfield as IL 56, North Avenue as IL 64. Turn ninety degrees and it's I-355 — the Veterans Memorial Tollway — with IL 53, 59 and 83 alongside.

Read that as a customer rather than as a driver and it explains why a barber in one village cuts hair for people who sleep in another. Crossing a border here costs eight minutes, so the useful question was never which town somebody lives in. It's whose name came up when they looked.
It's also why every page gets built for one thumb and one bar of signal. A great deal of the deciding in this county happens in a parked car.

sections.h2: Four services up here, and the same four again inside each town.
paras: The pages linked below explain how each part of the job works — what gets built and in which order, how the map decides who it shows and why, what a ledger holds once everything runs through it, and what becomes of a card payment between the terminal and your bank. None of those answers changes at a village boundary, so they get written once and written properly at this level.

The town versions are doing a different job. Each starts from the ground of one particular place: a business that already has customers and wants the searches it never appears in, a business working from a sign and a phone number, a village with three trading districts that behave nothing alike. Same service, different starting point, different advice.

So read whichever matches how you are thinking today. If you are still working out what any of this involves and what it costs, begin up here. If that part is settled and the question is how it plays where you actually trade, go into the town.

sections.h2: One owner, one bill, and nobody to introduce to anybody.
paras: This is built for the business where whoever unlocks the door in the morning is also whoever answers reviews at eleven at night. Two bays, four chairs, one van, a room with six tables.
If your signage came down from a franchisor, somebody is already doing this for you and a second vendor would only add a meeting to your week. That's a straight answer rather than false modesty.

Everyone else needs fewer suppliers rather than better ones — a single number that gets picked up when the booking page misbehaves, and an invoice that doesn't change shape from one month to the next.

sections.h2: Both prices, and they don't move between towns.
paras: Foundation sits at $250 a month, after a build fee of $250 paid one time. That's the website on your own domain, the Google Business Profile set up properly, booking against your calendar, Google Workspace email at your address, the local search work, and two updates a month.

Growth sits at $500 a month, after a build fee of $500, and adds the ledger: invoicing, payments, automated texts and emails, review requests, expenses filed where the income is, monthly reports, and a sync to whatever your accountant keeps the books in.

Pay the twelve months up front and 15 percent comes off — $2,550 and $5,100 respectively, setup billed separately, which reads as $212.50 and $425 a month. The bolt-ons are $100 a month for round-the-clock phone answering and $130 a month for automated Google review replies. Anything beyond that is priced to the job, in writing, first.

sections.h2: What we won't put in writing.
paras: Placement in Google's local results isn't for sale. A guarantee about a position on that map is therefore a promise about somebody else's product, and we won't sign one.
What does go in writing is the schedule: what happens to the profile, the pages and the reviews each month, and a report that says so plainly, including in the months it went the wrong way.

You also won't find a growth percentage anywhere on this page, or a chart pointing upward, or a story about what somebody's revenue did. The only numbers here are prices and census figures, and we would like it to stay that obvious.

pages.townPara: DuPage held 932,877 people at the 2020 Census, second-most of any county in the state, spread across 336 square miles with Wheaton as the county seat. Lombard is the closest of our three towns to the city and Wheaton the furthest out, with Glen Ellyn in between — which is where we work from. Between them they hold a good share of the county's owner-run businesses, and not one of those owners pictures their trading area as a county. They picture it as about a fifteen-minute drive, and everything below is built to that scale.

crmCallout.heading: One ledger, three towns, and no charge for crossing a border.
crmCallout.para: Ours keeps the appointment, the invoice it turned into, the expense that came off it and the date somebody is due back — one record per person, whichever village they sleep in. The alternative isn't a worse system, it's four systems that don't speak to each other: a diary by the register, a card reader's history, a contact list on a phone, and whatever anyone can still remember about last March. Every part of it is registered in your name and leaves with you.

cta.heading: Start with the service, or start with the town.
cta.para: Seven pages sit under this one — four services covering the county, and three town hubs carrying six trades and four services each. If testing something appeals more than reading about it, the demos are open, or (331) 291-7400 reaches whoever would be building yours.

faqs.q: Which towns have pages of their own?
faqs.a: Three of them: Glen Ellyn, Wheaton and Lombard, each with six trades and four services written for that town specifically. We work with businesses elsewhere in the county as well — the build is identical and so is the price, there simply isn't a page for every village.

faqs.q: There's a county SEO page and a town one. Which do I read?
faqs.a: Both, in that order, because they are not the same article twice. The county page sets out the mechanics — relevance, distance and prominence, and why a result shifts depending on where the person searching happens to be standing. The town page takes those mechanics and applies them to one place, for a business at a particular stage of its life. If you only have ten minutes, spend them on the county one, because it changes how you read everything else.

faqs.q: Does the price change depending on the town?
faqs.a: It does not. $250 a month with a $250 build on Foundation, $500 a month with a $500 build on Growth, and 15 percent off if the year goes in up front. Nothing about a ZIP code changes an invoice.

Glen Ellyn, one town east of Wheaton. We publish the village and the state and no street address. The practical part of being local is that we can stand in your shop for an hour before anybody designs anything, which is worth more than it sounds.
